analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from pooling landlord data to recommend rent prices to multiple owners.
analysis.headline: The bill to outlaw rent-setting software coordination was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a crime-level antitrust violation for a landlord to hire a company that pools rent and vacancy data from many landlords and uses it to recommend what rent to charge — the kind of service software companies like RealPage provide. It would let the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general enforce the ban, and let tenants sue for triple their damages. It has been referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters in markets where landlords use shared-data pricing software, especially tenants of large corporate landlords. The bill would give them FTC/DOJ/state enforcement, private lawsuits with triple damages and attorney fees, and the ability to bypass lease arbitration clauses to bring such claims. Small landlords competing with algorithmically coordinated big landlords could also gain a fairer market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, especially tenants of large landlords

how_it_helps.text: It makes it illegal for a landlord to pay a company that pools rental data from multiple owners and recommends rents, and illegal for any person to run such a service.
It deems that coordination an automatic ('per se') violation of the Sherman Act and an unfair method of competition the FTC can penalize.
It lets tenants sue for triple damages plus attorney fees, and lets them void pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in their leases for this kind of claim.
It relaxes pleading standards for price-fixing claims and preserves stronger state laws rather than preempting them.

analysis.who_pays: Large landlords and the rent-analytics software industry, which would lose the ability to sell or use pooled pricing recommendations, and could face FTC penalties, DOJ suits, and treble-damages class actions. Some of any compliance cost could be passed to renters in the form of higher operating costs, though the bill's premise is that rents would fall.

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches any platform that recommends rents to two or more landlords using pooled data, which could sweep in tools that help small landlords price competitively against large ones, not just schemes that push all rents up together.

Making coordination a 'per se' violation — illegal regardless of whether it actually raised prices — goes beyond current antitrust doctrine, which normally requires proof of harm, and opponents would argue that punishes lawful data analytics without showing actual consumer injury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted: it attacks a specific practice — centralized rent-price recommendation software — rather than capping rents, which avoids the tradeoffs of rent control. The costs fall on landlords and software companies that argue shared data can be legitimate (arguably an "entrenched" outcome for them only if the ban were badly designed). A fair trade-off for renters, though its fate in committee is the real question.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no amendments, and no vote — the usual resting place for bills leadership doesn't schedule.

narrative.text: Introduced November 19, 2025; the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action has been taken since the referral; the bill has not been scheduled for committee consideration or a floor vote.

All 12 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and with the bill sitting in a committee where it would likely need some Republican support to advance, it has gone nowhere.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and rent-setting software companies are better off so far, because the bill has not moved and their current practices remain legal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and pricing-software firms, so far

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Welch, Klobuchar, Booker, Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Van Hollen, Sanders, Shaheen, Smith, Kim, and Fetterman

against.name: Rent-setting software industry (e.g., RealPage and similar pricing-algorithm providers)
against.role: Vendor of rent-recommendation software facing federal price-fixing lawsuits
against.what_they_did: The bill targets the rent-recommendation software business; such companies have publicly defended their practices and fought related antitrust litigation, though no action by them appears in this bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on and none appear in the record supporting it.

industries.note: Companies that pool landlords' data and recommend rents would have their core business declared illegal. This is the bill's direct target.
Big multi-market landlords lose access to algorithmic rent coordination, which they currently use and which tenant advocates say pushes rents above competitive levels.
Renters gain both enforcement (FTC, DOJ, state AGs, private triple-damages suits) and a workaround-proof rule that arbitration clauses can't block.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee with no action since and no Republican cosponsors. Bills introduced this late in a session with single-party sponsorship and no committee movement almost never reach the floor; expect it to die in committee unless it is attached to a larger package.
